On the storm-damaged Achaean shore, Thestor stood over a heap of copper drift-bolts, his apprentice still blowing the coals beneath the goatskin hood. Three curved braces remained to be trued before sundown if the steersman from Euboea was to give them berth and the promised barley-meal. Yet the sea had cast up something that refused the hammer: a heavy cylinder of dark iron, thick as a bull’s shank, half-buried in wrack and gray gravel. Its surface pitted by sulfur rather than charcoal fire, the iron’s crust of compacted gray meal crumbled beneath his flat tongs.

Odysseus came over the shingle, his cloak pinned high against the brine-mist. The king bent neither knee nor brow, but his eye caught the fine, machine-turned lip where salt had failed to bite. He touched the lip with the pommel of his dagger, noting the bore that ran through without weld or fold. “Let’s haul this up,” he said, beckoning his bench-men to haul the iron up toward the council huts. 

The steersman, seeing the king’s hand upon the smith’s hearth and the sun tipping into the hills, cast off his painter and let the Euboean hull swing out into the gut of the bay. The apprentice looked toward the darkening sea; their wages lay uncollected on the bench, their ship was gone, and within the broken chamber of the iron remained only the gray ash of a flame that had never fed on wood.

The household’s passage was delayed, and Thestor incurred a household cost in time and wages. The damaged object, an unfamiliar weapon, complicated ordinary work. Odysseus witnessed a material clue but gained no complete understanding. The new development revealed an alien workshop pressing upon his chest, knowing that mortal tongs never drew such seamless weight from earth. The cost to household departure was clear, but the unanswered question hung in the air: What became of heroic honor when a man of little standing could strike down a champion beyond spear reach?
